newsitem.title: USA: Mortgage-backeds rise amid contained prepay fears.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage-backeds rise amid contained prepay fears.

text.p: Mortgage-backed securities (MBS) on Monday posted slight price gains which wavered in sync with Treasuries amid renewed confidence that prepayments would not speed up as much as market participants had feared.
"We certainly could see more people swapping back into mortgages from Treasuries" as prepayment hedge trades unwind, one trader said.
The market was subdued, however, ahead of retail sales and inflation data being reported Wednesday and Thursday.
Thirty-year MBS were unchanged to 6/32 higher, while 10-year Treasury notes rose 4/32.

Current coupon bonds from Government National Mortgage Association, Federal National Mortgage Association and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp were all up 3/32 at 100-30/32, 100-31/32 and 101-04/32, respectively.
Fifteen-year MBS were 1/32 to 5/32 firmer on the day, while balloon MBS were unchanged to up 2/32.
The Treasury 10-year note yield, at 6.35 percent, was holding well above the 6.00 percent to 6.10 percent threshold considered an essential prepay trigger.

Analysts were not ruling out the prospect of renewed prepayment pressure. Much hinged on the response to Wednesday's July retail sales and Producer Price Index reports and to Thursday's July Consumer Price Index data, they said.
Participants said that as the new data are released, they would scrutinize mortgage rates for more direction in assessing prepay possibilities.

The Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) released it latest weekly mortgage rates Monday. The net yield for a 30-year fixed-rate loan rose to 7.63 percent, excluding servicing fees, up from 7.45 percent a week earlier. The rate remained below the year-ago level of 8.01 percent.
